newsitem.title: UK: Metals Outlook--Markets stall as summer draws on.
newsitem.headline: Metals Outlook--Markets stall as summer draws on.

text.p: Base metal markets should be busier on Monday as interest returns to the London Metal Exchange (LME) after the lifeless end to last week, traders said.
But there were signs that some metals were starting to drag their heels anyway last week as the seasonally slow summer period dampened physical activity.
"Some of these markets are basing on the charts at the moment," one trader said.

Copper and aluminium would be looking to stave off declines under $2,400 and $1,600 a tonne respectively, having looked distinctly disinterested on Friday. Zinc might yet correct further from last week's 6-3/4 year highs, but lead could spark higher.
In copper, the run-up to the sensitive July date would see July premiums being maintained within the wider backwardation of $145.
Last Wednesday's July options declarations were somewhat inconclusive in that the market fell between strikes at $2,500 and $2,550.
However, there was no real relaxation in the spreads after the expiries, which suggested that the downside for futures prices would be restricted.
Analysts and physical traders said more metal appeared to be available, and that the market might veer lower once the July tightness had been defused.
Aluminium had been advancing steadily, but that trend petered out in the middle of last week, leaving the market struggling to stay above $1,600 in the absence of end-user business.

"The problem with the market at the moment is that with fundamental demand stable but unexciting approaching the summer holiday period, it is difficult to see it continuing upward from consumer interest if the specs stop their buying," another trader said.
Zinc, which stepped back from highs of $1,495 hit last Thursday and ended the week at $1,470, might correct lower further still.
Technical analysts saw a band of resistance between $1,495 and $1,530, so the correction could stretch back to $1,380.
But it was open to question whether would get that far as there were tightness storm-clouds looming for September.
Most of the good zinc stock was in strong European trade hands, and was not likely to be released, while the shorts were having quality problems in delivering, analysts said.
Lead might have further to run in the immediate short term after running up to three-month highs of $664 last Friday.
Traders said some consumers held off buying, and were having to buy now, given that prices were moving higher.

Also, the summer weather so far in Europe had been miserable, which could mean that the subsequent winter might be less favourable than recent years. All of which had positive implications for battery-maker demand, a trader said.
